item.title: Nvidia CEO boomerang reinforces IT worries about AI risk exposure
item.description:
Today’s move by the Nvidia board of directors is raising enterprise CIO concerns about AI over-reliance on one vendor, along with the question of whether boards can still effectively manage their CEOs, analysts and consultants said.

Despite saying last week that Jensen Huang was out for good, the board announced on Monday that it was reinstating him as CEO. 

One concern raised by the Nvidia statement is that of the direct involvement of US President Donald Trump in the board’s move.

“The Board received input from senior levels of the United States government and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk,” the statement said. 

Nvidia did not respond to a request for further details.

The statement worries Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research. “Nvidia said the quiet part out loud: Its board answers to more than just its stockholders,” he said. “When a board says its decision rests partly on input from senior levels of the United States government, Washington has a seat at the table.”

He added: “Nvidia’s release says the board received input from senior levels of the government. ‘Input’ is the word Nvidia chose. When the input comes from the government that writes your export rules, the line between input and pressure gets thin.”

Potential changes under interim CEO raised concerns

The brief tenure of Nvidia acting CEO Colette Kress had raised some concerns that she would revisit various Nvidia investments in other AI companies.

During a November 17 earnings call, Kress signaled that she might pull back, or at least reevaluate, some of those investments, especially in terms of financing data centers. 

“We remain thoughtful in how we participate and disciplined in how we commit capital. We are proud of the role that we have played so far in supporting the ecosystem,” Kress said. “As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments and guarantees.”

She added that Nvidia under her leadership would be “taking a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing, as a lot of things have changed over this last quarter,” and noted that Nvidia will engage in “a lot of work to understand if those are the right types of investments that we need to make.”

Some reassurance, for now

Dickson said Huang’s return could deliver some reassurance that no meaningful changes are imminent. 

“The larger AI ecosystem should feel the return most. Huang has been the bank of Jensen, financing the AI companies that buy Nvidia’s chips,” he said. “Nvidia’s own balance sheet shows it: non-marketable securities, its stakes in private companies, grew from about $22 billion in January to about $66 billion in late October.”

 But that comfort might be short-lived, as the board statement raised the possibility that the reinstatement might be reversed.

“As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation,” the Nvidia statement said. “The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.”

Dickson said that for enterprise CIOs, “Huang’s reinstatement is relief today. The investigation keeps the risk alive tomorrow. Jensen Huang’s return gives CIOs back the Nvidia they planned around.”

However, he noted, “It does not necessarily give them back certainty. That is a Sword of Damocles hanging over the CEO of the company at the center of enterprise AI. A second boomerang is possible.”

Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, added that the government involvement raised difficult questions. 

“Senior US officials gave the board enough comfort on the national security question to reinstate him before that investigation finished,” Kenney pointed out. “In other words, the government played a direct role in deciding who runs one of the enterprise market’s most important suppliers. CIOs should expect Nvidia’s leadership and product availability to remain closely tied to US policy.”

Removed some Board independence

Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, however, voiced concerns that “part of the pressure that reversed [the CEO decision] came from the state. That gives the decision weight and takes away some of its independence. Procurement leaders who count on board oversight as a backstop have reason to feel less reassured. Boards of critical suppliers must publish the reasons for leadership decisions, including the ones they reverse.”

And Brian Jackson, a principal research director at Infotech, was even more blunt. 

“The Nvidia board’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO looks like a cave-in to external pressure rather than doing what’s truly best in the long-term interests of the company,” he said. “In the Nvidia statement about putting Huang back into his role, they say that discussions with the US government assured them that his reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

However, he noted, “at the same time, the Board says it will continue investigating the matter. So which one is it? Is the doubt about being compromised by a foreign intelligence effort cleared or is it under investigation? The statement also does not acknowledge the alleged breach of conduct involving Huang’s reported affairs with two Nvidia employees. Their silence risks leaving employees uncertain about how seriously the Board takes the boundaries between personal and professional relationships.”

Highlights risk of over-reliance

The biggest single concern expressed by consultants and analysts was about the way this decision highlights the extreme enterprise IT risks associated with over-reliance on a handful of key AI companies. 

Pam Baker, AI consultant at consulting firm Human Interrupted, said that it adds several items to customers’ to-do lists.

“For CIOs buying from these companies, a supplier that can lose hundreds of billions of dollars in a morning because of one person is a supply-chain risk,” she said. “Diversify, tighten contracts, and add governance to vendor due diligence. The bottom line: when boards can’t check the CEO, the CIO’s controls over access, records and data may be the last safeguards still working.”

Kenney agreed. 

“Enterprises already have a vendor-concentration problem with Nvidia. The last eleven days showed that some of that exposure also sits with one person,” he said. “Nvidia’s technology continued to work, but its leadership, market confidence, and government relationships changed quickly because of Huang’s conduct. The Board even indicated they would not bring Huang back, but reversed course after pressure from shareholders and government, which highlights how critical of a role Huang holds in the organization. That adds key-person risk to the vendor risks that CIOs need to consider going forward.”

Dickson added that Monday’s reversal should remind CIOs that they need to treat even the largest AI vendors as they do the smallest startup.

“CIOs should ask every supplier the question they used to save for startups: ‘What happens if the founder walks out the door tomorrow?’” Dickson said. “Keep AI workloads portable enough that a leadership shock at one vendor is a headline, not an outage.”

And Stephanie Balaouras, a VP/group research director at Forrester, noted that the announcement changes the leadership picture, but not the strategic advice.

“The concentration risk still remains what it is,” she said. “Although Huang’s reinstatement may calm immediate concerns around Nvidia’s leadership, it should not reverse enterprise efforts to build alternatives into their AI infrastructure strategy. Restoring leadership does not mean restoring confidence in resilience. Leaders need to keep confronting AI concentration risk.“

item.title: AI-powered, customer-first thinking drives CRM advantage
item.description:
Organizations are redefining CRM with AI-enabled systems that deliver highly personalized, responsive customer experiences and create competitive advantage. Yet technology on its own isn’t enough to power the transition. Organizations need a partner willing to go beyond the generic playbook to align CRM transformation with strategic priorities and measurable business goals.

Simply adding AI on top of legacy CRM isn’t the fix for creating end-to-end, autonomous workflows that free sales reps from tedious manual data entry work or enable customers to self-serve with action-oriented, personalized experiences. Sales and customer experiences built around legacy CRM are hampered by silos that cause friction and propagate incomplete and stale data. Without real-time, dynamic intelligence about customer needs and behaviors, organizations remain reactive, perpetuating long-standing challenges such as inconsistent experiences, slower resolution, and missed opportunities.

“AI changes the role of CRM,” says Andrew Gaeckle, senior partner, platforms and customer strategy practice lead at West Monroe. “It’s no longer just a place to store customer information or track interactions. It can help people decide what to do next, prepare for a conversation, and handle parts of a service request.”

CRM’s new role comes with new demands for both the technology and implementation partners. Specifically, organizations need a more unified approach to AI-powered CRM that delivers real-time intelligence coupled with an implementation strategy intentionally synced to desired business outcomes and ROI.

From a partner perspective, that means shifting emphasis from AI add-ons to channeling the technology to solve real business needs. “Partners can’t stop at configuring the platform,” Gaeckle says. “They need to understand the business processes around CRM, whether data is reliable, how work moves between teams and systems, and how to measure whether changes are paying off.”

West Monroe and ServiceNow: partners for AI-era CRM

ServiceNow’s AI-native Autonomous CRM platform is built from the ground up to support modern CRM workflows, creating a single source of truth and action across enterprise operations. With the unified data model and architecture, workflows tap into consistent data from any system, applying AI automation to streamline work across customer sales, service, and sales and operations.

West Monroe combines business and industry expertise with process transformation, data integration, AI enablement, and deep ServiceNow delivery experience to facilitate CRM transformation and tailor solutions to individual companies’ operating models and priorities.

Among West Monroe’s core differentiators are:

  • Deep industry expertise. Not all customer journeys are the same. West Monroe’s rich experience across healthcare, utilities, manufacturing, insurance, private equity, and financial services ensures CRM initiatives are linked to specific business outcomes and ROI. “Our industry experience helps us account for the workflows, regulations, and expectations that shape what will actually work,” Gaeckle says. “We keep the solution grounded in a client’s business rather than treating CRM as a generic software rollout.”
  • A focus on connected front- and back-office operations. A great customer experience depends on what’s happening behind the scenes. If a representative can’t see the status of an application, claim, order, or service issue, new and improved CRM screens won’t fix the problem. West Monroe considers how the front office connects to operations, data, and other systems to deliver promised experiences.
  • Human-centered design, from the outside in. West Monroe starts by understanding what customers and employees are trying to do, identifying where there is friction. Processes and technology are shaped around those needs. This human-centered design approach leads to more useful solutions, which in turn builds trust in AI-enabled CRM workflows and drives adoption.

The results speak for themselves: Customers across industries are reporting a wide range of outcomes, including 20% lower churn, 33% faster resolution, and 40% faster quote processing.

As a global business and technology consulting firm, West Monroe emphasizes customer value by co-creating solutions that accelerate intended outcomes. With proven results across a range of industries, West Monroe ensures AI-enabled CRM becomes a strategic lever for growth.

To learn more, visit westmonroe.com/partnerships/servicenow

item.title: Jensen Huang returns as CEO of Nvidia
item.description:
Nvidia’s board of directors announced Monday that Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO of the company. Huang resigned on November 12 after it was revealed that he had had multiple extramarital affairs, including with a woman who is being identified as a suspected Chinese spy.

Huang has received strong support from other tech leaders, including US President Donald Trump, and has himself said he was open to return. However, as recently as last week, the board said the door was closed for Huang.

Now they are backing down, partly because they do not see Huang as a risk to US national security.

“During the decision-making process, the board received input from senior levels of the U.S. government, and based on these inputs, the board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement does not pose a risk to national security,” the board wrote in a press release .

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Nvidia’s newly appointed chairman of the board, in the release. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company.”

In a statement, Huang said it is an honor for him to return to Nvidia.

“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the Nvidia board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading Nvidia during this period,” Huang said in the statement. “I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.” 

Nvidia shares, which had already shot up in premarket trading following the announcement, opened 30% higher. 

This story originally appeared on ComputerSweden.

item.title: The FAA outage is a warning about technical debt in the AI era
item.description:
The search for a single culpable company in the November 13 nationwide ground stop risks missing the point. Investigators are examining a Juniper Networks router installed by FAA contractor L3Harris, which says it is cooperating with the inquiry. As of November 19, the precise cause remained unresolved. Accountability matters. But identifying who triggered the disruption will not, by itself, explain why the wider system was so vulnerable. 

According to the FAA, a flood of network connection attempts destabilized legacy equipment, disrupting communications and radar feeds. Blocking traffic from two facilities stabilized the network. In my view, this bears the hallmarks of accumulated technical debt—the hidden burden of past shortcuts and deferred fixes. The investigation needs to explain both what initiated the failure and what allowed it to spread. 

The November 16 banking disruptions bring that second question closer to home for businesses. Chase attributed its difficulties to a software bug, while customers at other banks experienced delays in transactions involving Chase, even where their own banks’ systems were working normally. Whether technical debt contributed remains to be established. But the disruption illustrates how a problem inside one organization can spread through the connections others depend on. 

Technical debt makes legacy systems increasingly fragile

Technical debt is what builds up when we take shortcuts, patch things together, rely on outdated components and put off improvements. It happens in software, electronic hardware and the connections between them. Things still work, but they become harder to maintain and upgrade. Change one part, and you’re not quite sure what else might break. That’s the interest we pay on the debt. Businesses keep adding to it whenever getting the next feature out the door takes priority over fixing what’s already there. 

Think of a house built in the 1970s. Over time, its owners add appliances and a bedroom air conditioner. Running the microwave and air conditioner together trips a breaker, so everyone learns not to do that. Then a licensed contractor adds a second floor, further straining the electrical system and introducing roof seams that can leak onto the patchwork of wiring in the attic. The family learns to watch for leaks whenever it rains. The unresolved problems and workarounds are its technical debt. Now imagine using AI-generated plans and recruiting thirty neighbors to build two more wings over a weekend. Everything seems fine on a pleasant spring day. But would you trust it on a 110-degree afternoon in Austin with every air conditioner running, or during a downpour? That is my concern about AI-generated code added rapidly to legacy systems without experienced engineering oversight. The analogy is not a claim that AI is causing the recent outages. It illustrates the challenge businesses face as they use AI to expand systems whose limitations they may already struggle to understand.

AI can accelerate development — and deepen technical debt

My research with Geoffrey Parker and Burcu Tan examines this challenge through interviews with software professionals and a dynamic simulation model. AI-assisted coding can accelerate development. But our interviews also identify duplicated code, dependency conflicts, outdated components and architectural mismatches. Code can perform its immediate task while making the broader system harder to maintain and change. 

Our simulations suggest that growing technical debt can swallow up AI’s early productivity gains, especially when new code interacts with legacy software. Our interviews suggest that working with electronic hardware can make these problems even harder to manage. Each new layer of complexity makes the next change more difficult. Eventually, developers spend so much time keeping things working that they have little time left to fix what’s causing the problems.

This does not mean businesses should reject AI-assisted development. Our model suggests a balance in which AI improves performance without allowing technical debt to overwhelm the gains. That balance depends on the environment. A short-lived prototype built from scratch presents a different problem from software expected to operate for decades alongside older systems. 

Preserving AI’s gains requires investing in engineering discipline

For business leaders, coding speed alone is an inadequate measure of success. A team can deliver features faster while increasing future maintenance obligations. Managers need to assess the cost of operating, modifying and integrating software alongside the speed of producing it. 

They also need to give technical-debt reduction dedicated resources. Our research suggests that sustained investment in retiring debt can help preserve AI’s benefits. If maintenance is always postponed until after the next release, the backlog can become a constraint on every future release. 

Experienced engineers are essential to this work. Their knowledge helps them recognize when apparently functional code conflicts with the architecture around it. Businesses should preserve that expertise, train junior developers to evaluate AI output, and document older systems before institutional knowledge disappears. Testing must examine interactions and failure conditions, including whether one component’s abnormal behavior can disrupt others. 

The FAA investigation may establish an equipment defect, an installation error or another explanation. Those findings will matter. But the broader lesson for businesses is already worth confronting. Replacing a component and strengthening a system are different tasks. The rush to modernize with AI makes understanding that distinction more urgent. We can generate software faster than ever. We must also invest in understanding, repairing and testing the infrastructure on which that software depends.

item.title: IT leaders aren’t sold on outcome-based software pricing
item.description:
AI and traditional software vendors have begun experimenting with pricing models tied to outcomes, but IT leaders largely remain wary of the change.

Some SaaS providers have explored outcome-based pricing due to competition from AI-based tools, but IT leaders say the emerging cost model leaves them with many questions. CIOs say sticking to budgets may be more difficult with outcome-based agreements than traditional software pricing models, and the new approach may set up huge disagreements over defining good outcomes between customers and vendors.

Although outcome-based pricing hasn’t caught on yet, IT leaders should be prepared for its nuances and challenges, says Manuj Aggarwal, founder and CIO at AI software vendor TetraNoodle Technologies.

“Outcomes are the right north star, but pricing every seat on an agreed outcome is hard when the outcome depends on people, data quality, and process change the vendor does not control,” he says.

An outcome-based approach forces vendors to define success in business language, not feature lists, something Aggarwal sees as an advantage. When the outcome is measurable, attributable, and mostly in the vendor’s control, outcome pricing can be a strong incentive to deliver, he says.

But outcome-based pricing will make software budgets unpredictable, Aggarwal adds.

“Attribution fights start — ‘Was that the model, the data, or the team?’” he says. “Teams game metrics, and finance loses a clean forecast. If the outcome needs human judgment under pressure, a pure outcome contract pushes risk onto the CIO without giving control.”

Solid idea, questionable result

Sachin Gupta, senior IT manager at a global electronics distribution company, likes the idea of outcome-based incentives, but he’s wary of the billing model.

“Outcomes are absolutely the right way to judge software,” he says. “Nobody buys a planning tool for the licenses; they buy it for better forecasts and fewer stockouts. So I understand why CEOs and CFOs like hearing, ‘You only pay when it works.’”

But attribution for outcomes is a major challenge, he adds. “Say forecast accuracy goes up eight points after we roll out an AI tool,” he says. “Was that the tool? The master data cleanup we did the same quarter? Or just a calmer demand cycle?”

At many enterprises, outcomes come from data, processes, and several systems working together, Gupta adds. “Pinning the result on one vendor is rarely clean, and that’s where the arguments start,” he says.

In addition, the outcome depends on who’s doing the measuring, he notes. “If the vendor’s own dashboard defines the outcome, they’re grading their own homework,” he explains. “Any outcome clause I sign has to be measured in our system of record, against a baseline we agree on before go-live.”

One of the main benefits of outcome-based pricing is that it gives customers a lower barrier to entry because they don’t have to commit to a big license contract before seeing results, says Andy Boettcher, CIO of AI and data infrastructure consultancy DoubleTrack.

But he also sees outcome-based pricing as a half-baked trend, particularly when pushed by AI vendors.

“It’s a marketing buzzword that could technically work, but only if the outcome is defined precisely and the effort that it takes doesn’t get spent,” he says. “And one of the most common failures with AI I see is that it fails having a clearly defined purpose that has no clear answer to ‘What do you actually want to accomplish with this?’”

The downside of the approach is everything that happens after the lower barrier to entry to AI software, Boettcher says.

“AI systems don’t answer the same way twice because they’re running different processing and logic with their equations — and models change and update all the time,” he adds. “You’re paying for outcomes that depend on many factors you can only control so much, and there’s significant risk.”

Idea hasn’t taken off

The good news for those IT leaders skeptical of outcome-based pricing is that it’s still in the early proof-of-concept stage. While AI vendors are moving from per-seat pricing to other models, including consumption and output pricing, outcome-based pricing represents a small percentage of the market, says Josh Sandberg, partner at management consulting firm Bain & Co.

Only about 10% of AI-native software vendors and seat-based SaaS vendors that have introduced hybrid pricing now rely on outcome-based meters, Bain & Co. says in an August blog post coauthored by Sandberg.

Because of the costs involved in delivering AI solutions, vendors have looked to tie pricing to some kind of usage metric, including outcomes, but use-based models can create headaches for customers, Sandberg says.

“Anytime you start talking about usage-based, you get into all these challenges of a budget predictability and forecastability,” he explains. “All of that gets even worse when you start talking about outcome-based pricing because it does get very tricky to come up with a good baseline for outcome-based pricing.”

While outcomes are the ultimate goal, they are difficult to pin down, he adds.

“To actually agree on what a real outcome is and how do you actually attribute that outcome to a software product that you’re buying, as opposed to many, many other confounding variables in the business, starts to introduce a whole lot of complexity into the buying process and into the budgeting process for customers,” he says.

Outcome-based pricing for AI tools has taken off in only one industry vertical, contact centers, Sandberg adds. Resolution of a customer contact is a relatively straightforward determination, he suggests.

A second potential use case for outcome-based pricing involves software packages that directly touch dollar flows, such as procurement or cloud infrastructure management, he says. “Vendors will say, ‘We can actually track baseline, and here’s what you would have spent because we’re actually measuring the dollars that are coming in and out, and we can measure the decisions that our software suggests in order to save you money,’” he adds.

Despite the limited use cases so far, Sandberg expects outcome-based pricing to slowly expand as vendors continue to experiment.

“It will be very use-case specific where one vendor has to go first and work through enough of these nuances and details to really get to a customer and industry accepted definition of what that outcome looks like, and then you see a tipping point,” he adds.

A good contracting process can also achieve similar benefits for software customers as the goals of outcome-based pricing, he notes.

“Think about doing a POC and making sure that you as a buyer are actually seeing value before you commit to a longer-term contract,” he says. “There are a lot of other contracting best practices that can help deliver some of the same goals that you would want to get as a buyer out of outcome-based pricing, but maybe with a little bit less of the incremental complexity.”

item.title: 3 key answers for CIOs as trust in AI still raises questions
item.description:
Now in its fourth year, the Thinkers360 AI Trust Index examines the current state of trust in AI from both an AI end user and AI provider perspective, and as an annual pulse check on sentiment across various aspects of trust.

The primary research survey was conducted, in conjunction with Babson College and Innogentic.ai, in Q3 2026 among Thinkers360 members and the global community of AI end users and providers. This year’s findings showed the overall AI Trust Index score for 2026 was 303 on a scale from 100 (not concerned) to 400 (extremely concerned).

Because higher scores reflect heightened anxiety, this persistent reading, close to last year’s score of 307, demonstrates that apprehension around AI risks remains high. So here are three key takeaways as CIOs continue AI implementation journeys into 2027.

1. Continuously benchmark trust scenarios and attributes

Like trust in general, trust in AI is multi-faceted and shifts continuously across all measurement dimensions. This means your given industry, use case scenarios, and attributes by which trust in your solutions and services is measured will shift as the industry, customer perspectives, and your own implementations evolve.

This year, the AI Trust Index found that media scenarios were of the highest concern, followed by personal, government, and workplace scenarios in terms of the percentage of respondents who were most concerned. Breaking this down further, AI end users and providers cited cybercrime, misinformation, and surveillance as the three areas where they were very or extremely concerned.

The area with the least concern was where AI is explainable and interpretable, yet even in this area, only 16% of AI end users and providers weren’t concerned.

CIOs should, therefore, monitor how their specific industry is perceived by customers, and how various AI trust attributes such as privacy, security and resilience, validity and reliability, safety, accountability, and transparency are valued. It’s vital to pay attention to all attributes and understand how they stack up in order to allocate resources accordingly. 

2. Move AI governance upstream

While we know lack of AI governance can directly impact customer and employee trust of AI solutions, the AI Trust Index found something more insidious. Trust in AI starts eroding earlier in the lifecycle as AI initiatives move from concept to value.

Concern about procedural, operational, and financial trust jumped from 52% at the AI idea and intake stage, to 70% at the AI use case and governance stage, and to 76% at the AI ROI and performance stage. Similarly, those stating they had complete trust dropped from 19%, to 12%, and to 7%, respectively, as AI initiatives moved through the implementation lifecycle from ideas and intake, to use cases and governance, to ROI and performance.

To improve AI governance and trust in AI initiatives it’s important to move processes upstream starting with AI ideas and use cases, effectively introducing a shift-left posture for trust in AI. This means evaluating and accounting for risk at the idea intake stage, and quantifying how governance and related costs may impact your overall return long before development resources are committed.

3. Close the AI trust gap between organization and customers

A surprising finding from last year was only 65% of AI end users either somewhat or strongly agreed that the benefits of AI outweighed the risks, compared to 83% of AI providers. The AI providers were clearly more bullish on the technology than end users.

This year, however, the gap has closed significantly to 72% of end users and 71% of providers. This is a promising sign AI end users and providers are more unified about the potential of AI: end users are becoming more positive, and providers more realistic.

The main takeaway for CIOs is to always read the pulse of your customers and address their concerns. Just as products come with user guides and safety manuals, ensure you provide customers with adequate training and education related to how your products and services support AI safety and governance. Provide this via your consulting services organization, if you have one, and via sales and marketing materials, or refer them to trusted partners and suppliers.

Even when an AI system is categorized as low-risk, meaning it escapes strict statutory mandates under frameworks like the EU AI Act, proactively educating users and customers about AI limitations such as exceptions, inaccuracies, and hallucinations is a critical best practice for user trust, brand protection, and liability mitigation.

Overall, it’s important to continuously monitor trust in AI and adjust or reset assumptions, expectations, and beliefs up or down accordingly. AI is moving rapidly on all fronts and even for more skeptical or pragmatic CIOs, it can be useful to revisit what you may have passed over or dismissed as not ready since a lot can happen in a short amount of time.

item.title: Claude, Copilot and Agentforce are ready. Are your SAP and ServiceNow platforms ready?
item.description:
At a 2027 planning session in October, I watched a leadership team approve three AI agent pilots in under ten minutes. The three were a claims-intake agent, a collections agent and a finance close assistant, each with a sponsor, a vendor quote and a slide of projected savings. The next item on the agenda was the SAP clean-core program those same agents would run on. It took forty minutes, drew questions about payback and slipped to 2028.

Nobody in the room did anything wrong. The agents came in as an operating expense from the innovation fund and were judged on speed to value. The clean-core program came in as a capital project and was judged on a three-year payback—two committees, two tests, one dependency that neither test could see. The agents were funded. The platform they would run on was not.

Versions of that meeting play out in most of the programs I advise, from banks to state Medicaid agencies. It is the planning mistake I see most often this budget season, and you can fix it before January.

Here is the number that should frame 2027. Gartner forecasts worldwide IT spending will reach $7.35 trillion next year, up 15 percent. Much of that growth will never reach your budget directly. By my arithmetic on the forecast’s own table, data center systems add $487 billion ($879 billion to $1.37 trillion), about half of the $961 billion increase, as cloud providers and AI labs build capacity. The same forecast expects “memflation,” its term for AI-driven memory price inflation, to persist through 2027 and push up server and PC prices. Take out the data center build-out and worldwide spending grows 8.6 percent, still more than double typical enterprise budget growth, because it also counts consumer devices and higher hardware prices.

Meanwhile, Gartner’s CIO survey puts average enterprise IT budget growth at 3.7 percent, up from 2.8 percent last year. Gartner notes that, after inflation, that is flat or negative in many countries. Funding for agentic AI rises an average of 31.8 percent, the fastest of any technology area. When one line grows more than eight times faster than the budget that holds it, the difference comes from somewhere else. In the programs I advise, it usually comes from the platform and run budgets agents depend on. IBM’s study of 2,000 technology executives expects AI to rise from just under 15 percent of IT budgets in 2025 to nearly 25 percent by 2027. Yet 85 percent of those leaders still lack full visibility into real-time AI spend.

The providers’ build-out will come back to you, too, as per-token, per-action, and per-user pricing. The real question for 2027 is whether agent money arrives with the money for the platform it depends on.

Vipin Jain

What actually breaks?

When AI and the platforms beneath it are funded on separate tracks, four things break (Figure 2). Each one maps to a discipline your CFO already applies to every other investment, which is why this is a budget problem before it is a technology problem.

Dependency

An agent is funded without the platform work it needs. At a Fortune 500 insurer, finance wanted an intercompany reconciliation agent on SAP. The pilot worked in a sandbox and stalled in production on years of custom code wrapped around the close: user exits, modified standard objects, interfaces nobody had documented. The agent could read the data. It could not act on it through a released API. The business case had counted the license and the build. It had not counted the remediation. The discipline that breaks is total cost of ownership.

The SAP ecosystem has been plain about this. SAPinsider warned in August that custom code, not data, is the hidden blocker for Joule agents, because core modifications turn every quarterly agent update into a re-testing project. SAP’s decision to make Anthropic’s Claude a primary reasoning and agentic capability across its portfolio raises the stakes, not lowers them. If you still run SAP ECC 6.0 on a current enhancement package, mainstream maintenance ends in December 2027. The deadline and the agent now point at the same line item.

Duplication

Every agent rebuilds the same plumbing. At a large bank, the first Salesforce agent carried the full cost of its integrations, test suites and monitoring, and the second team started from zero because nobody had funded those pieces as shared services. Consumption pricing makes duplication visible faster than seat pricing ever did. Salesforce meters Agentforce at $0.10 per action through Flex Credits, so a poorly designed agent pays for every redundant step. The discipline that breaks is amortization. Each agent pays for investments that should be spread across many agents.

Fragmentation

The business context lives in the tools, not in the enterprise. At a healthcare payer, three AI tools ran on three definitions of “authorization.” One sat in the core administration platform, one in a vendor’s prompt library, and one in a spreadsheet maintained by a clinical operations lead. Every new use case meant another round of rework, and every vendor switch would have meant losing the definitions entirely. The discipline that breaks is asset ownership. The most valuable thing an AI program produces is a governed version of what your business means. That is the strategic edge a CEO is paying for, and in the programs, I see, it often sits inside someone else’s product.

Opacity

The organization cannot say what a completed piece of work costs. On a state Medicaid program, the first agent invoices arrived as token counts. Budget officers could see the bill rise but could not connect it to cases processed, backlog reduced or errors avoided. The conversation turned from value to fear in a single meeting. Token prices keep falling, yet in the programs I advise, the cost of a completed task keeps rising as agents add reasoning steps, memory and guardrails. The discipline that breaks is unit economics. Until you can price a completed workflow, you cannot defend one.

In every one of these cases, the agent itself worked. What failed was the funding around it.

Table 1 puts the four cases side by side.

An agent funded without its platform is not an investment. It is an option you have not paid for.

Vipin Jain

Why doesn’t the budget process catch it?

Because it works exactly as designed. Most enterprises run two investment paths. Innovation money moves fast, tolerates uncertainty and rewards visible pilots. Platform money moves slowly, demands payback and rewards risk reduction. Agents travel the first path. Clean core, integration and data foundations travel the second. Neither process asks whether one depends on the other.

The pricing models make the comparison harder. Microsoft prices Agent 365 at $15 per user per month. Salesforce sells Agentforce through per-action Flex Credits. Model providers price by token. Platform work is priced in project hours. A budget committee looking at those four units cannot tell which costs belong to the same outcome, so it approves them one at a time.

Ownership has drifted too. Deloitte found in its survey of 3,500 leaders that 40 percent of companies already let AI execute decisions or actions without human approval to at least a moderate degree. For 23 percent, accountability for a bad outcome remains unclear, and an agent nobody owns has no budget owner either. The Cloud Security Alliance reports that 82 percent of organizations have discovered previously unknown agents in the past year, and only 21 percent have a formal process for decommissioning them.

The public sector feels it most sharply. The 2026 NASCIO State CIO Survey found that only 28 percent of state CIOs have dedicated funding for AI initiatives. CIOs are again calling for a move away from the inflexible chargeback model that bills agencies for IT services. Chargeback was built for a world where a person in one agency consumed one service. An agent working a case across three agencies does not fit that model, and neither does its bill.

What has the market already conceded?

What strikes me most this year is how quickly everyone converged. Model makers, platform vendors, cloud providers, service firms, standards bodies and analysts landed on the same message within months, as Figure 3 shows. Each has conceded that agents need a control plane, shared context and cost management underneath them. Each would like that layer to be its own. The agents are productized. The foundation is where the competition and your bill now sit.

Vipin Jain

The platform vendors moved fast. In April, Google introduced the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the evolution of Vertex AI, to run and govern agents at scale. Microsoft made Agent 365 generally available on May 1 as a control plane for agents built in Copilot Studio, Foundry and beyond. At Knowledge 2026 in May, ServiceNow announced an expanded AI Control Tower to govern agents wherever they run. SAP followed at Sapphire in May with its Anthropic partnership. By Dreamforce in September, Salesforce had Agentforce Coworker generally available and Claudeforce, its Anthropic partnership, in beta. OpenAI launched Frontier in February to build, deploy, and manage what it calls AI coworkers, initially for a limited set of customers. In September, AWS moved Amazon Bedrock Managed Agents into preview. It is an AWS service, developed jointly with OpenAI.

The service firms followed the gap. Anthropic, Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman and Goldman Sachs launched an enterprise AI services firm in May. When a model maker helps fund implementation capacity, it signals the bottleneck has shifted from the model to the enterprise around it.

Standards and trade groups are filling in the rest. The Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation already hosts MCP, and in October Anthropic donated its Agent Skills standard to it. The FinOps Foundation reports that 98 percent of its survey respondents now manage AI spend, up from 63 percent in 2025 and 31 percent in 2024. Managing a bill is not the same as seeing it in real time, which is the 85 percent gap IBM found.

The analysts read the same signals. Forrester issued the sharpest warning, calling SAP’s Autonomous Enterprise vision credible. In the same breath, it warned that anchoring on Claude creates concentration risk that becomes a board-level issue in regulated industries within 24 months. McKinsey’s guidance to banking CIOs describes a North American bank where each new agentic coworker inherits the infrastructure, controls and lessons learned from the ones before it.

Looking forward, the dated commitments cluster early. Salesforce said at Dreamforce that its long-horizon agents would reach general availability in November. SAP plans general availability for the SAP Enterprise AI Gateway and new SAP Knowledge Graph capabilities in the first quarter of 2027. Two hard deadlines then close the year: SAP ECC mainstream maintenance and the EU’s high-risk AI obligations, both in December 2027. Most vendors have not published anything firmer for 2027, which is itself a planning signal. Fund for capabilities you can see shipping, and treat everything else as an option.

That has a commercial edge. When several vendors compete to run the same workflow, your bargaining power comes from portability. Ask every vendor in your 2027 renewals whether its agents speak MCP, whether agent definitions and logs can be exported, and what it costs to move a workflow to another platform. A vendor that cannot answer is pricing in your lock-in.

Does the political climate change the plan?

Mostly, it changes the timing. In Europe, the Digital Omnibus on AI, in force since July 27, moved the AI Act’s stand-alone high-risk obligations from August 2026 to December 2, 2027. Obligations for AI embedded in regulated products moved from August 2027 to August 2028. The new date lands inside your 2027 roadmap. In the United States, the December 11, 2025 executive order launched a federal push to preempt state AI laws, but as of late October, Congress had not enacted any federal preemption. Until Congress or the courts settle it, plan for state AI laws to keep applying.

Cost has a policy side too. Tariffs add volatility to hardware already squeezed by memflation, so price next year’s refresh with a buffer. Data sovereignty rules increasingly determine where an agent may run and which model it may call, which is another reason to keep models swappable. In the public sector, the November 3 elections produced 19 new governors, and only 40 percent of state CIOs keep their jobs through a governor transition. Many 2027 state CIOs will inherit agent programs funded under someone else’s assumptions.

The practical answer is architectural. Build controls into the platform once and configure them by jurisdiction, rather than building compliance into each agent. Programs built this way absorb a new rule with a configuration change, not a rebuild.

Where should CIOs start?

None of this requires a new governance body. The leaders I see getting ahead are doing six things in order, starting with the two or three workflows where they can afford to learn.

  1. Start from the business plan, then tag every AI dollar to a workflow. Begin with the three or four outcomes on the CEO’s 2027 plan, not with the AI backlog. Then attribute existing AI spend to the business process it serves before approving anything new. IBM found that organizations with strong AI financial discipline deploy 2.4 times more AI agents with no higher AI or IT budget.
  2. Pair every agent with its platform dependency. One line item, one accountable owner, one business case that includes the clean-core, integration or data work the agent needs, whether the platform is SAP, Salesforce or ServiceNow. This is the change that fixes the insurer’s close.
  3. Fund the shared machinery as a product. The integration layer, test suites, guardrails and monitoring get their own budget and product owner, and every new agent consumes them. The test is simple: the second agent should cost less than the first.
  4. Own the context, buy the plumbing. Buy models and orchestration from the market, whether Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft or Amazon, and keep them swappable. Build your business vocabulary once, govern it like a data product, and keep it in-house. At the payer, one governed definition of authorization ended the rework that came with every new use case.
  5. Release autonomy in stages. As Figure 4 shows, start with a human approving every action, move to sampled review as accuracy holds, then to exceptions only. Record each step as a decision with supporting evidence. Plan the role changes in the same quarter, or the agent will quietly redesign them for you. Deloitte reports that 60 percent of companies have redesigned jobs around AI to at least a moderate degree, but only 15 percent describe the change as extensive or complete.
  6. Price by the completed workflow, and retire something every quarter. Report cost per case, per claim or per close, not per token. Use the savings from retired custom code, duplicate tools and failed pilots to fund the next step.

Vipin Jain

The gates between those steps are what make the roadmap real. On the Medicaid program, moving from full approval to sampled review required three months of accuracy data and a cost per case inside target. Moving to exceptions only requires a recorded decision by the program director. When we started reporting cost per case processed, the budget conversation moved from fear of the bill to the value of the work. In the public sector, where every dollar is appropriated, and every decision about a beneficiary can be audited, that evidence is what makes an agent defensible in front of a legislative committee.

Figure 5 shows the shape of a balanced 2027 roadmap, adapted from the ones I am building with clients now. Every quarter, fund AI and platform work together, and every quarter ends with a gate.

Vipin Jain

Take the roadmap to the board as one portfolio with three numbers: the share of AI spend tagged to a workflow, the cost of a completed workflow and the cost of each new agent compared with the first. If those three move in the right direction each quarter, the program is working, regardless of the agent count.

The takeaway

The CIOs who come out of 2027 ahead will be the ones who funded agents and platforms in the same line and made every agent cheaper than the last. That reframes the job for this planning cycle: half portfolio manager for AI bets, half architect of the platforms those bets run on.

It also means saying no in the budget meeting. Decline the agent that arrives without its platform dependency funded. Decline the clean-core program that arrives without an agent or a business outcome attached.

None of this is new. It is the pattern I have watched for thirty years, from trading floors to Medicaid programs. When business strategy, technology and the way people work are planned on separate tracks, technology industrializes the gap between them. Agents industrialize it faster.

So, ask your team three questions this week. None of them requires a program to answer.

The agents are ready. Fund the platform they will run on.

The CAF is a leadership community of the IASA, the leading non-profit professional association for business technology architects.

item.title: Could AI data centers help with the US senior housing crisis?
item.description:
Two seemingly unrelated trends are creating major infrastructure challenges in the United States. One is familiar to virtually every CIO; the other may be less so.

Less familiar, America’s demand for senior living communities is rising faster than developers are building them. The oldest baby boomers turn 80 this year, and the shortfall of senior housing units is growing more severe. According to NIC MAP’s 2026 Senior Housing Market Outlook, the need for additional senior housing will reach approximately 576,000 units by 2030 and exceed one million units by 2035 if construction continues at its current pace.

Much more familiar is the rapid expansion of AI data centers and their effects on

surrounding communities. A 2026 report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory projects data centers could account for 11.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption by 2030, up from an estimated 4.7% in 2024. With new facilities being proposed across the country, growing electricity demand, water consumption, noise pollution and more have created widespread community concerns.

What if these two challenges could help address each other?

Data centers generate enormous amounts of heat that must be removed so servers can reliably operate at or near peak performance, but creative planning can turn this heat into a valuable resource for nearby residences, potentially reducing heating expenses and demand for additional energy. The underlying technology is already working in Europe, and a proposed development in Chicago offers a glimpse of how it could be adapted in the United States.

I believe there’s an opportunity to take this idea further by exploring partnerships between data center developers and senior housing operators. In the right circumstances, these arrangements could reduce heating costs and create new revenue opportunities to help make senior housing more affordable for our most populous generation as they enter their golden years.

Excess heat as a community resource

Cooling is a fundamental requirement of data center operations, and historically, data centers have rejected heat into their surrounding environments, whether through air cooling, evaporative cooling or other methods. Liquid cooling is increasingly being incorporated into data center designs to accommodate the higher power requirements of AI infrastructure. In any of these scenarios, removing heat offers an opportunity to use it rather than simply discard it.

In Groningen, the Netherlands, data center operator QTS has partnered with local energy provider WarmteStad to supply recovered heat to a district heating network. As CIO has reported, the system uses heat pumps powered by renewable energy to circulate hot water through an existing underground district heating network that supplies residual heat to 10,000 households, buildings and knowledge institutions.

Both sides receive something useful. The community gets access to a heat source that would otherwise be discarded, and the data center benefits from the cooling provided through the energy exchange.

This approach is not always appropriate. The engineering requires more than connecting two buildings. Data center cooling systems generally operate at temperatures below those required for conventional building heating. Heat pumps would likely need to raise the temperature, and a distribution network must transport the energy to where it can be used.

Still, Groningen demonstrates how data center heat capture can become part of a community’s energy infrastructure, and the United States is beginning to explore similar opportunities.

In Chicago’s Bronzeville neighborhood, for example, developers have proposed Metropolis Pointe, a mixed-use development combining a data center with residential, commercial and community facilities. Griffin Venture Group, the project’s developer, announced additional infrastructure milestones in August 2026, including plans for a 170,000-square-foot data center and a 42,000-square-foot central utility plant. The proposed utility system would integrate heating and cooling across the campus with the goal of reducing energy costs for residents.

Although still in the proposal stage, Metropolis Pointe’s design reflects an important evolution in thinking as developers begin to consider how infrastructure can support the needs of neighboring communities and buildings.

If this approach can work for conventional residential developments, it can likely be applied to improve the lives of our growing senior population.

A new partnership model for senior housing

Senior living communities may be particularly well suited for this.

They operate 24/7 with substantial year-round energy requirements. Heating, hot water, kitchens, laundry facilities and common areas all contribute to operating expenses, and in colder climates, traditional HVAC or electric heating can be an especially high cost.

As high energy costs persist in the United States and across the world, construction costs have also increased, financing remains costly and challenging, and many older Americans cannot absorb higher housing expenses on their fixed budgets.

NIC MAP estimates that meeting future senior housing demand will require more than $1 trillion in cumulative investment through 2050. Hopefully efforts to close that gap will incorporate new approaches to development and financing, not just more of the same accepted inefficiencies.

I envision at least two potential opportunities for data center developers to help.

First, heat recovery can reduce operating expenses. A senior living community located near a suitable data center could potentially receive recovered heat through a shared thermal network, offsetting some of the energy otherwise purchased for heating and hot water. For residents, benefits would depend on how savings are shared, but lower utility expenses could help operators manage costs to moderate rent increases or provide discounted or no-cost services.

Savings could also result from real estate and infrastructure partnerships. Senior housing developers with available land might be able to lease a portion of their land to a data center operator to create an additional revenue stream. Developers could also plan complementary facilities together to share and thus lessen energy infrastructure and development costs.

Any projects should be carefully planned. Large hyperscale data centers won’t always be appropriate. I think smaller computing facilities and strategically located data centers and developments connected through district heating networks will prove more practical.

Data centers would still need adequate space, zoning, electrical capacity and commercial demand to make each arrangement work, but the potential of lowering operating expenses and adding revenue should be carefully considered. The United States needs to expand senior housing capacity, and it would be nice to lessen the cost burden on our seniors.

As communities demand more in return for hosting large data centers, jobs and tax revenue are important, but these benefits can be difficult for residents to realize directly. Helping support housing for older Americans with data centers could provide a more tangible connection between digital infrastructure investment and community needs.

Economics and engineering

Can this promising concept lead to viable projects? I think so but certainly not for every data center or every senior living community. It’s a matter of identifying opportunities where economics, infrastructure and community needs align to provide ideal situations to test at least two models that may prove worthy to expand over time.

On one hand, brownfield opportunities could be identified within existing senior housing developments. Multi-state operators could evaluate their portfolios to identify facilities with available land, suitable heating systems and the necessary access to electrical infrastructure. In the right situations, smaller computing facilities could be added with limited disruption to provide additional revenue and deliver recovered heat into the community’s existing energy systems.

Retrofitting older facilities can be expensive. Potential savings would need to justify investments, but a careful audit could reveal promising and otherwise overlooked opportunities.

On the other hand, new facilities could be developed collaboratively from the outset. Chicago’s Metropolis Pointe development offers an early example of this integrated approach even though it’s not designed specifically for seniors. When envisioned together, creating the ideal infrastructure could make all the difference.

If data center developers and senior housing developers form partnerships and identify ideal sites together, heating, cooling and distribution infrastructure could be designed around the needs of both facilities rather than attempting to connect systems after construction. With the greatest flexibility, this greenfield approach could create opportunities to share infrastructure costs, establish long-term energy agreements and potentially generate lease revenue that helps supplement and support senior housing.

In either case, recovered heat must be available at useful temperatures, and there needs to be enough seasonal demand. Water use, security, noise and other community concerns would need to be addressed, but careful site selection and integrated design advantages could go a long way.

Ideally, a small number of promising projects could test the models, measure their results and demonstrate where these partnerships can deliver meaningful benefits.

The U.S. senior housing shortage is too vast for any single innovation to solve, but as investment in AI infrastructure continues to accelerate, we have an opportunity to think more creatively about how that infrastructure can contribute to the well-being of its surrounding communities. If thoughtful engineering and strategic partnerships can help reduce housing costs for seniors, support new development and make data centers more welcome, environmentally friendly neighbors, I think it’s an opportunity worth pursuing.

item.title: Hyring Insight Reports 10x Revenue Growth in 3 months
item.description:
Hyring’s newest workforce intelligence platform has grown 10x in revenue in just 90 days.

Hyring, the emerging AI hiring platform, which to date has run 900,000 plus AI interviews, announced that its new product, Hyring Insight, has grown tenfold over the last 90 days. The company’s quick success comes from two key product decisions: transparency and Ask AI, an aide that helps explain what employees did during the workday.

Hyring Insight is time tracking software that prides itself on transparent employee monitoring. It tracks their working hours, their activity, and the apps and websites they use, along with screenshots while the timer is running, and it uses artificial intelligence to explain where the workday went and what was achieved.

AI-Generated Timesheet Insights

A timesheet can tell managers if eight hours were worked. Hyring Insight predominantly uses AI to analyze the workday. Its Ask AI feature answers questions regarding time and activity. It holds back on making any final decisions about a person.

There are four plans for clients to choose from. Free covers up to two users with 30 days of history included. They can then choose to upgrade to the Starter plan, the Pro plan, which gives automatic AI summaries, time-lapses, and alerts, or the Enterprise plan, which is built for enterprises with 50 or more users and adds remote vs office statistics, a read-only AI connector, SSO, SCIM, an audit log, API, and a custom DPA. If a client chooses annual billing, they save up to 30%.

For paid plans, unusual activity is activity that differs from the employee’s own pattern, which may include any input that seems artificial. Each flag must be verified at the manager’s discretion, as Hyring Insight makes no recommendation.

For employees, the app includes an avatar, streaks, music, and kudos from other colleagues. No badge or streak can be earned by working overtime, and this data is never used in performance reviews.

Built to be Trusted, Sold to be Retained

The one thing that Hyring Insight never does is run when the timer is paused. The platform does not log individual keystrokes, keep track of any sensitive data like passwords or messages, or access the camera or microphone. Employees can at any time view their own data on their web portal, the same data that their managers will see.

“Our work revolves around product innovation and how much clients value the product,” says Adithyan RK, Chief Executive Officer of Hyring. “Employee monitoring software that is resented by the people who use it never gets renewed. We built Hyring Insight so that any employee can see their data exactly as their manager sees it. The transparency of it all is why teams keep it, people trust it, and that is what turned our early momentum into a viable business.”

About Hyring

Hyring is an AI hiring platform headquartered in Chennai, India, founded in 2022 by Adithyan RK and Surya N. Its products include the AI Video Interviewer, AI Resume Screener, AI Phone Screener, AI Coding Interviewer, English Proficiency Test, and their latest, Hyring Insight, which is an employee monitoring software. More information is available at hyring.com.
